narrative:
The model predicted an 83% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. First, your plan to attend law school part-time was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Among accepted students, only 7% planned to study part-time while 93% planned to go full-time; the model sees full-time focus as much more likely to lead to passing the bar.

Second, your third-year grades placed you in the third decile of your class, noticeably lower than the average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students. This weaker academic performance in the later years of college also pulled the prediction toward failure.

Third, your family income being in the middle bracket contributed a smaller but still negative nudge. While many accepted students also come from middle-income families, the model has learned that this bracket, when combined with the other factors, slightly increases the risk of not passing the bar.

Taken together, these elements led the system to conclude you were unlikely to pass on the first try. To improve your chances, consider reapplying after switching to a full-time program, strengthening your later-year grades if possible, or gaining additional academic or test-prep experience that demonstrates readiness. This would directly address the factors that most hurt your current profile. (218 words)
